extracted.intended_audience: scholars and students of philosophy/aesthetics, comedy studies, and performance; critics and informed practitioners of stand-up comedy
extracted.subtask_description: Critical/philosophical analysis of a stand-up special (Hannah Gadsby: Nanette) that extracts evaluative criteria for comedic practice and for assessing how comedy handles trauma, self-deprecation, structure, and audience connection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-deprecatory humor (definition and dual character)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Self-deprecating humor... is humor in which a comedian makes themselves the butt of the joke.” It is familiar and widespread and can be endearing and effective at connecting with audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can function positively (signals humility, helps audiences relate, can be strategic or playful). But when it stems from genuine shame or self-loathing it is detrimental — especially for performers from the margins, where self-deprecation can be a symptom of humiliation. Examples: early female stand-ups who used it to gain entry; anti-pattern: repeated self-put-downs that reveal genuine shame. Use carefully: assess whether self-deprecation is a ruse to expose target ignorance or a harmful internalization that sacrifices performer wellbeing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-deprecation as strategic ruse vs genuine humiliation
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-deprecation can be a façade used to 'reclaim power and assert authority' or it can be evidence of real humiliation and self-hatred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When strategic, self-deprecation can 'allow the speaker to adopt what is essentially an authoritative stance without alienating the majority of the audience' (Russell). Use small, insincere jabs to lighten load and build trust; avoid material that requires silencing one's trauma or prioritizing audience laughs over self-worth. Example: Gadsby uses self-deprecation playfully in Nanette to create openings for truthful material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jokes vs stories: necessary structure for conveying trauma
rubrics_metrics.description: “Stories... need three parts. A beginning, a middle, and an end. Jokes only need two parts: a beginning and a middle.” Jokes are setup + punch line; stories afford closure and are better for conveying whole traumatic experiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For traumatic material, favor story forms that provide endings and emotional resolution rather than reducing events to setup+punchline. Anti-pattern: freezing formative experiences into repeatable joke-routines that fuse with memory and prevent healing. Use longer-form narrative when the aim is being heard or forging connection rather than merely eliciting laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punch lines and closure (limits of punchlines)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The feature that distinguishes a joke... is a punch line.” Punch lines often leave a question for the audience to answer and typically do not provide closure like tragedies or full stories do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that punchlines produce openness rather than resolution; that makes them ill-suited to conveying complete accounts of trauma. When evaluating or composing material, consider whether a punchline's openness is ethically or artistically appropriate for the subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tension creation and dispelling (comedian's role)
rubrics_metrics.description: The comedian’s job is traditionally to create and then dispel tension, but a performer may intentionally create tension and refuse to relieve all of it: 'Gadsby... is able to create a highly successful and very funny comedy show in which she completely controls the tension while explicitly choosing to leave significant portions of it with the audience.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tension strategically: building trust first, then introducing dangerous/edgy material. Leaving some tension unresolved can be purposeful (to teach, provoke reflection, or transmit the weight of trauma). Anti-pattern: habitually diffusing all tension so that traumatic significance is erased. Evaluate whether unresolved tension serves the ethical/aesthetic aims of the piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition, pain, and distance (Libera's three elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Libera's 'working hypothesis' isolates three elements that together create comedy: recognition, pain, and distance. 'Comedy is not necessarily defined by laughter' but by calibrating these elements to get a response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing/evaluating a set, consider how recognition (relatability/reference), pain (emotional or risky content), and distance (psychological separation that makes the incongruity manageable) are calibrated. Use recognition/call-backs to build rapport before introducing painful or distant material; miscalibration can alienate or traumatize audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punching up vs punching down (power dynamics of targets)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy's moral valence depends on power relations; mocking the powerful ('punching up') can be morally instructive, while 'punching down' at marginalized targets often perpetuates harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer targets where ridicule calls attention to abuses of power. Anti-pattern: making marginalized people the butt of jokes in ways that reinforce their marginalization. Example: Gadsby mocks patriarchy and powerful figures (punching up), whereas earlier comedy often targeted those 'who exist in the margins.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of anger in comedy (gendered expectations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Angry comedy is familiar and often lauded when performed by (white) men; women and performers from margins face constraints and expectations to perform self-deprecating humor instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess audience expectations and institutional biases: angry material can be powerful and morally instructive, but performers from marginalized groups may face backlash. Consider strategies (narrative framing, earned trust) to introduce anger without simply being dismissed or penalized by audience preconceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical handling of trauma (do not prioritize laughs over wellbeing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Performers should not prioritize audience pleasure over their own self-worth or the truth of traumatic experiences: 'the pleasure of the audience is not enough to compensate for her pain.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When presenting traumatic content, include truth/closure where necessary, avoid eliding harm for laughs, and be mindful of the personal cost of repeatedly performing traumatic material. Anti-pattern: routine-ifying trauma into punchlines that re-traumatize the performer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stand-up set structure includes non-joke material and narrative arc
rubrics_metrics.description: Stand-up is not merely a sequence of jokes; sets tend to be highly structured, often including non-joke material, beginnings/middles/ends, and narrative sense across the performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design sets with an arc: use early relatable material to build trust, space laughs, use call-backs and callbacks/repetition, and place taboo/difficult material where the audience is prepared. Recognize that non-joke material can be central to achieving effects beyond instant laughter (connection, reflection).

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity reactions (three audience responses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Morreall's taxonomy: three general reactions to incongruity—comic amusement, negative emotion, and puzzlement. The same incongruity can produce different reactions depending on individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating/composing material, anticipate varied audience reactions: amusement (enjoyment), puzzlement (leading to thought/learning), or negative emotion (distress/urge to act). Material that aims at social change may deliberately seek puzzlement or negative emotion rather than pure amusement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience connection and trust-building before pushing boundaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedians 'rarely start off with their most taboo or challenging material' but first establish a connection so audiences give leeway later; play sympathetic/relatable characters early to enable darker moves later (halo effect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with material that creates recognition and rapport. Use that trust to introduce riskier or more didactic content. Anti-pattern: opening with taboo without groundwork, which risks alienation or misunderstanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter as social stimulus (provine's observation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical observation: 'the critical stimulus for laughter is another person, not a joke' — much laughter arises from social interaction rather than strictly joke-like stimuli.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factor social dynamics and performative presence into evaluations: timing, delivery, interpersonal cues, and audience-performer contagion can be more important than propositional joke content. Assess live performance differently from transcripted jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy contract and permissible deviations
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an implicit 'comedy contract' (expectations about setup/punchline and tension resolution); artists may break or stretch it to new effect: 'Gadsby doesn’t break the comedy contract, but instead stretches and bends the contract.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that departures from conventional contract (e.g., refusing to relieve tension, narrativizing trauma) can succeed artistically and ethically if thoughtfully constructed. Evaluate whether deviations are purposeful, coherent, and achieve intended connection or critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ridicule vs hatred: target's power and the moral meaning of laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato/Aristotle distinction: ridicule is appropriate for ignorant/weaker figures whose faults are 'not painful or injurious'; hatred is appropriate for powerful figures whose ignorance causes harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether laughter at a target is morally appropriate by considering the target's relative power and the injuriousness of their faults. Anti-pattern: laughing at serious harmful behavior as if it were trivial (e.g., reducing violent bigotry to buffoonery when it actually injures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of repetition and call-backs for recognition and connection
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition (call-backs) and reference-humor produce recognition; recognition can be 'very effective in producing laughs' and creating connection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ repetition/call-backs to build rapport, anchor themes, and allow risk-taking later. Beware overuse that flattens emotional impact or masks unresolved trauma.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calibrating unresolved tension for pedagogical or political effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaving tension unresolved can be intentional: 'the tension that lingers holds the promise of changing minds and changing behavior.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the goal is social change or ethical reflection, consider deliberately refusing to dissolve certain tensions so audiences feel the discomfort of marginalized experiences. Evaluate whether unresolved tension is ethically justified and whether it is likely to produce reflection rather than mere alienation.
